The Hudson River. Flowing approximately three hundred fifteen miles southward from the Adirondack Mountains in upstate New York to New York Harbor and the Atlantic Ocean, the Hudson is one of the most historically and culturally significant rivers in North America. Though relatively short, it has served as New York City's principal waterfront and a major symbol of American commerce and industry. The river originates in the Adirondack Mountains near Lake Tear of the Clouds in a pristine wilderness region. The English navigator Henry Hudson explored and sailed it in sixteen hundred nine while seeking the Northwest Passage, giving the river his name. The Hudson forms the boundary between Manhattan and New Jersey for much of its course through New York City. It created the first major American settlement at New York Harbor, making it essential to colonial commerce and later becoming the busiest port in North America. The river is subject to significant tidal influence all the way up to Troy, New York, making it partially a tidal estuary rather than a purely freshwater river. Historically it has been heavily polluted from industrial development and contaminated with PCBs, though ongoing restoration efforts seek to revive its ecology. In the nineteenth century the river inspired American landscape painters of the Hudson River School, including Thomas Cole and Frederic Church, securing its place in American artistic tradition.
